content:
Joseph Santamaria is general manager of energy and utilities at Amazon Web Services. The U.S. economy is facing a looming shortage of electricity on the grid. With energy demand projected to grow more than 50% by 2050, utilities are under growing pressure to keep up. The problem isn’t a lack of new energy projects. In the United States, more than 2,000 GW of potential power projects are waiting to be reviewed — enough to power every home in the country more than twice over. The challenge is bringing those projects from planning to execution. Before utilities can bring new sources online, they must complete interconnection studies. These technical reviews determine how and where new power sources can safely plug into the existing grid. Each study takes months to complete, and projects can wait years just to reach the front of the line. In the early 2000s, the average project waited about two years. Today, surging power demand has more than doubled the wait to five years and counting. New AI-powered grid tools can help shorten the time to approval by completing these studies in hours instead of months. With power demand growing rapidly, using new technology to speed up the approval process is critical to fueling economic growth, meeting demand from essential industries, and keeping electricity affordable and reliable for everyone. Where a traditional study might test a handful of what-if scenarios one at a time, AI tools can model thousands of them at once by testing how new projects interact with the existing grid, including its power lines, substations and generators, across multiple scenarios. These systems run thousands of simulations to generate recommendations while human engineers make the final decision. With machines performing the legwork, operators can evaluate new projects much more quickly. Utilities that have invested in AI grid tools are already seeing results. Duke Energy, the largest utility in the country, has used AI-powered grid planning to reduce study time while doubling the number of projects evaluated in a year. On the West Coast, Pacific Gas & Electric pulled together data from more than 80 sources across 20 different systems into a single planning tool, helping prioritize more than 17,000 upgrades across the grid. The program cut costs by 20% within a $100 million pilot program and eliminated millions of customer outage minutes. Regulators are paying attention, too. This summer, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission brought together utilities, tech companies, government agencies and others to discuss how AI can speed up grid planning. It's a clear sign that regulators see AI as a potential solution to grid backlog. The urgency is clear. Increased demand from across the electric grid, from electrification to renewable energy projects to AI data centers, is adding pressure to an already backlogged system. Critics have raised questions about whether new facilities will drive up costs for existing customers or worsen the approval bottleneck. The answer depends on how these projects are structured. When large energy users cover the cost of new infrastructure and utilities use modern planning tools, everyone benefits. In Indiana, an agreement between Amazon and Northern Indiana Public Service Co. is expected to deliver approximately $1 billion in savings to existing customers over 15 years, with Amazon covering all costs associated with building new data centers. Research from the Electric Power Research Institute confirms that with the right planning and pricing rules, new demand can help keep electricity prices in check. These deals work best when utilities can evaluate and approve projects quickly enough to meet demand. That's where AI becomes a key player not just as a driver of new demand, but as the tool that makes it possible to bring new power demand onto the grid while shortening the time that everyone waits in line. The utilities moving first on AI-powered grid planning are delivering real results — faster approvals, fewer outages and lower costs. For the communities where this new energy infrastructure is being built, that means reliable power and stable electric bills. The longer utilities stick with outdated planning processes, the longer families and businesses wait for the energy they need.

[s0001 0:00] Context windows have grown from well, a few thousand tokens to well, a lot bigger like a million or more. And that's room for more stuff, more instructions, tool results, docs, you name it. So, if we think about AI agents and we give them access to this big old context window,
[s0002 0:28] well, they should probably be get getting better at long-running tasks, shouldn't they? I mean, the more context, the better job they can do. Well, a recent study looked at 18 frontier models and it turned out that they all got less reliable as the context window got bigger. Researchers have taken to giving this thing a name and that is context rot. The more tokens in the window, the less reliably the model uses any of
[s0003 0:58] them. And this is the problem that context engineering is there to solve. Context engineering is deciding what actually goes into this context window at each step of an agent's run. Now, there are many ways an agent's context can go wrong and I'm going to cover four of them, the four failure modes that you can encounter when working with these big context
[s0004 1:26] windows. And because I'm feeling nice, I'll also suggest how to fix each one. And the funny thing about those fixes is they involve deliberately throwing away information. So, how does an agent get better and by holding less context? Well, to answer that, we should first take a look at what's actually filling up these giant context windows. So, let's say an AI agent was given the job to migrate an aging codebase over to
[s0005 1:55] a new database driver. So, I'm talking about here, we are building a migration AI agent. Now, at the beginning of the context window, the first thing most likely in here is the system prompt. That's the standing instructions for how the agent operates in general. Now, the agent task itself, that will also be stored in here as well, just as
[s0006 2:24] a prompt on its own. And it might not be very big. It might only be a couple of lines. Then, many agent harnesses also pull in a bunch of project instructions. Now, these are things like an agents.md file explaining how this particular project is built. Then, after that, we might have some tool definitions, a description of every tool the agent can call.
[s0007 2:51] And from here on in, the context window turns into a bit of a running log. So, we're going to have a message history here. This is every step the the agent has taken. And after, let's say, an hour of running, well, this could get pretty big. That's going to be a lot of steps. And then, the biggest band is probably the tool results that we store here, which is things like file contents and
[s0008 3:19] test output and error logs and schema dumps. So, the job description, the prompt, is a few lines near the front, and pretty much everything else is the stuff that the agent kind of piles up along the way. Oh, and buried in this as well, there happens to be a note. This is a note the agent wrote itself. It says that the new driver retries failed connections automatically, so the
[s0009 3:46] old retry code can be deleted. So, the note just basically says, "Hey, don't bother with writing any retry code." Why do I mention that? We'll come back to that. Anyway, why is a a full context window a problem? Well, a model doesn't look things up in its context the way a database looks up a row. Every token in the window is competing for a finite
[s0010 4:14] amount of attention, essentially an attention budget. And to me, this is kind of the crux of it. The window might hold a million tokens, but the attention spread across those tokens is finite. Now, what about those failure modes? Let's start with the first one. Number one, that is context poisoning. So, I cryptically mentioned the agent
[s0011 4:42] wrote itself a note about the new driver retrying failed connections automatically. Well, it turns out that that note is completely wrong. The agent shouldn't have done this. It basically skimmed the driver's documentation, it misread it, and then it's written down a false conclusion. And that's all poisoning is. A mistake gets into this context window somewhere, and then gets treated as fact because to the AI model, its own notes, they look
[s0012 5:10] like the ground truth. So, file after file our agent has been deleting perfectly good retry code. Next, number two, that is context distraction. This is where the sheer size of the history starts steering the agent. Now, a language model at its heart is just a pattern continuation machine, and when the context holds at say an hour of an agent's own past actions, that history
[s0013 5:40] becomes pretty much the strongest pattern around, stronger than the reasoning it picked up in training. So, instead of asking what the job needs next, the model might drift into doing more of what it has already done in this message history. Agents in this state can get stuck just kind of going over old ground. What about number three? And that is context confusion. And this one comes from the tools.
[s0014 6:09] Our agent here is wired into quite a lot of stuff. There's probably some amount of version control here. There might be access to a database console. Maybe it also is logging tickets into a ticketing system. And each of these tool definitions is in the window whether it actually gets used or not. And having more of them makes choosing the right tool a bit harder.
[s0015 6:37] And in one benchmark, a model failed a task when it was offered 46 tools, but it then passed the very same task when it was only offered 19 tools. That is tool sprawl at work. Okay, number four. That is context clash, which is when the window contains information that disagrees with itself. So, take that note with the bad information. At some point our agent is going to see
[s0016 7:06] that no retries are happening and it's going to figure out that that note was wrong. And it will probably make a note of that into its message history as well. But the problem then is we now have both versions sitting in the window that are presenting conflicting information. So, these are four different ways a context window can go bad. All right. So, what about some potential fixes? Well, for poisoning, one of the fixes
[s0017 7:36] is to validate. Before a conclusion gets written down into this context window, check it against something real. So, one quick connection test and our agent would never have written this no retry code note. What about distraction? Well, the fix there is really to compact. When the history gets really, really long, the agent can summarize it.
[s0018 8:06] Which is to say it throws the full log away and starts again from the summary, a a shortened version of what was in this message history in the window. Now, compaction is lossy. A summary of a summary can start to drift like a photocopy of a photocopy. So, consider moving as much out of the context window as possible and put them into permanent files instead. Detailed information can be retained in those files and then it
[s0019 8:35] can be pulled into the context window only when it's actually needed. All right, what about context confusion? Well, that is a curation problem. So, the fix is to curate. The agent doesn't need 46 tools for database migration. So, just give it the handful that the job calls for and then it can always go and fetch others if it actually needs them. Then finally, context clash. Well, the
[s0020 9:05] fix there can be to prune. So, when information gets superseded, just delete the old version rather than leaving both in the window. We could have deleted this guy entirely. Or go further and start a fresh window just restating the current corrected state of the job and leave the poisoned stuff behind. So, if a false conclusion gets saved, that's poisoning. So, you can validate. If the
[s0021 9:34] history has taken over, that's distraction, so compact. If the agent has more tools than the task needs, that's confusion, so curate. And if the context disagrees with itself, that's a clash, and the fix is prune. And all four fixes work by throwing something away. An agent can get better at long tasks by holding less. Now, I'd love to know how you keep an
[s0022 10:02] agent's context lean. Do you have your own context engineering fixes? Let me know in the comments.
